title: Fit the last magnet into a motor rotor, holding down the loose magnet beside it so it cannot jump out
instruction: Fit the last magnet into the motor rotor: take the red-topped magnet from the wooden tray (the poles must alternate red, blue, red, blue around the rotor) and put it into the empty slot, pressed in flush with the rotor's top. The blue-topped magnet in the slot next to it is loose and will jump out toward the new magnet as it comes near, so hold it down with your other hand until the new one is in. Then let go and take both arms back to where they started.
context: Electric motors for robots, cars and drones are built by pushing strong neodymium magnets into slots in a steel rotor, with the poles alternating. Neighbouring magnets pull on each other hard enough to drag a freshly placed magnet out of its slot, chipping it and pinching fingers, so assemblers hold the last magnet down while the next one goes in.
setup: A table in front of two arms (bases 61 cm apart), seen by one overhead camera and a camera on each wrist. Distances are measured forward from the line between the arm bases and sideways from the midpoint between them. (1) A motor rotor: a stack of dark silicon-steel laminations 20 cm across and 5 cm tall, its axis 30 cm forward on the centre line, with a steel shaft stub 2.5 cm across standing 4 cm above it, on a fixed aluminium fixture plate 25 cm square and 8 mm thick. Four rectangular slots 4.6 by 2.0 cm run down through the stack, their middles 8.5 cm from the axis, at 24 and 36 cm forward, 6 cm left and 6 cm right of the centre line, each running along the rim. (2) Four magnets' places: in the slots at 36 cm forward, a red-topped magnet (left) and a blue-topped one (right), each set in amber epoxy resin; in the slot at 24 cm forward and 6 cm left, a loose blue-topped magnet standing flush with the rotor's top, not glued; the slot at 24 cm forward and 6 cm right is empty. Each magnet is a nickel-plated neodymium block 36 by 12 by 50 mm (160 g), its north face painted red and its south face blue. (3) A beech tray 12 by 5 cm, 1 cm thick, centred 28 cm forward and 20 cm right of the centre line, its long side running forward to the right at 45 degrees, holding two magnets upright in 1 cm deep pockets, each turned the way the empty slot runs: a blue-topped one at 26 cm forward and 18 cm right, and a red-topped one at 30 cm forward and 22 cm right. The loose magnet and a magnet from the tray pull toward each other (red over blue) or push apart (blue over blue) with 8.5 N at 11 cm between their middles, falling as the fourth power of the distance, at most 12 N; at about 6 to 10 cm above the empty slot a new magnet lifts the loose one out unless it is held down. The steel round the empty slot pulls a magnet whose bottom is within 2 cm above its mouth onto the slot's middle line and down into it. The layout is the same in every trial, as in the screenshot.
scoring: Judged at the end, except the jump, which counts at any time. Jumped: the loose magnet rose more than 6 mm in its slot at some point. Flush: the red-topped magnet in the empty slot, upright within 8 degrees, its middle within 6 mm of the slot's middle line across and 9 mm along, its top within 4 mm of the rotor's top. 1.0: the red-topped magnet flush, the loose magnet never jumped, and both arms back where they started (each gripper's fingertip centre (TCP) within 5 cm of its start); 0.5: the red-topped magnet flush and the loose magnet never jumped; 0.25: either magnet at least half its height inside the empty slot; else 0.0. The trial ends at the run limit, or once the full score has held for 1 s with the red-topped magnet and the loose magnet still.
reset_notes: Pull the new magnet out of the slot and stand both tray magnets back in their pockets; push the loose magnet back down flush in its slot.
fidelity: Rigid-body simulation (Isaac Sim 6.1, PhysX, 20 Hz control). Simplified: the magnets' pull is a force along the line between the loose magnet and each tray magnet (1/d^4, capped at 12 N); the two potted magnets pull on nothing. The steel's pull near the empty slot is a centring force. The rotor and its fixture are one fixed body. Cameras 1280 x 704 (Dream-1 sees 320 x 176).
